content:
Facts: A father brought proceedings against his daughter, alleging that his deceased mother had transferred the bare ownership of her sole immovable asset to the granddaughter by means of an apparent sale that in reality concealed a donation. He claimed that the act infringed his rights as a forced heir and sought a declaration of nullity for lack of form and, alternatively, reduction of the concealed donation. The defendant did not appear. It emerged during the proceedings that the plaintiff had not accepted the inheritance with benefit of inventory.

Legal framework
Articles 536–537, 553–564 ICC on forced heirs and the action for reduction; Article 564 ICC on the requirement of acceptance with benefit of inventory; Articles 1414 ff. ICC on simulation; consolidated case law on the relationship between actions for simulation and reduction.

Interpretative issue
Whether a forced heir who alleges simulation of a sale concealing a donation, and who substantively seeks reinstatement of the reserved share, may bring the action without having accepted the inheritance with benefit of inventory, and whether the formal framing of the claim as one for nullity avoids the applicability of Article 564 ICC.

Principle applied
Where the overall content of the claim shows that the plaintiff is substantively seeking reinstatement of the reserved share through reduction of a donation (even if concealed by a simulated sale), acceptance of the inheritance with benefit of inventory is a condition of admissibility under Article 564 ICC. The formal qualification of the claim as an action for nullity or simulation does not circumvent this requirement. Confused or repetitive pleadings that ultimately pursue reduction lead to inadmissibility if the statutory prerequisites are not met. Accordingly, all claims were declared inadmissible.
